description_full: Eurobank S.A. provides retail, corporate and private banking, asset management, treasury and capital market, and other services in Greece, Bulgaria, Cyprus, and Luxembourg. It operates through Retail, Corporate, Markets, International, and Investment Property. The company offers current accounts, savings, deposits and investment savings products, credit and debit cards, consumer loans, small business banking, and mortgages, as well as overdrafts, loans and other credit facilities, foreign currency, and derivative products. It also provides custody and clearing services, cash management and trade service, and investment banking services, including corporate finance, and merger and acquisitions advice services. In addition, the company offers financial instruments trading and services to institutional investors, as well as specialized financial advice and intermediation services; and mutual fund products, institutional asset management, and equity brokerage services. Further, it is involved in investment property activities related to a portfolio of commercial real estate assets. Additionally, the company engages in the provision of business-to-business e-commerce, accounting, tax, sundry, leasing, factoring, investment banking, asset management, brokerage, informatics data processing services; real estate business and real estate services; fund management; insurance agency and brokerage services; general and life insurance; pension assurance intermediary business; and production and distribution of solar generated electric energy. Eurobank S.A. was founded in 1924 and is based in Athens, Greece. Eurobank S.A. was formerly a subsidiary of Eurobank Ergasias Services and Holdings S.A.

financial_summary: EUROBANK S A is a large-cap financial services business with a $17.4B market cap on $3.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

The business throws off $2.9B in free cash flow — roughly 78 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 33% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
